text: 74 2.6. Ecuador 2.6.1. Fire danger in 2024 The danger of forest fires in Ecuador in 2024 was strongly influenced by its bioclimatic characteristics, which vary considerably due to the country’s geographical and climatic diversity. During the dry season, regions such as Sierra, Costa and, to a lesser extent, the Amazon, showed a significant increase in the likelihood of forest fires occurring, especially in a reas disturbed or degraded by human activities, which became highly susceptible to ignition. In the particular case of the Amazon region, while fires were recorded in degraded areas or during extreme weather periods, their overall vulnerability was lower compared to the Sierra or the Coast, where the recurrence of forest fires was higher due to topographical, social and climate factors. Ecuador has 91 ecosystems distributed throughout its territory (Ministry of the Environment, Water

title: JRC143555_02

Among those most affected by forest fires were: — Arable and shrub asparagus. — Tropical dry forests. — Montane forests. — Forest plantations of exotic species such as eucalyptus and pine. The latter, generally located in urban -forestry interface areas or agricultural areas, acted as highly flammable vegetable fuels, especially during the dry season. Its chemical composition – rich in essential oils – the accumulation of loose litter and the lack of proper forestry management increased the risk of fire spreading, exacerbated by the improper use of fire in farming practices. Climate change Ecuador’s geographical and complex terrain, combined with the influence of oceanic phenomena such as El Niño and Humboldt’s current, have generated a remarkable climate diversity in the country. In contrast to well - marked stations in temperate regions, Ecuador has alternating rainfall cycles and droughts, mainly influenced by the Andes Cordillera. This mountain range determines the distribution of rainfall, causing abundant rainfall in the west and drier conditions in the orient area. The phenomena of El Niño and La Niña exacerbate these variations, generating respectively heavy rainfall or droughts in different areas. This climate variability has contributed to a great diversity of ecosystems, from the Amazon to the Andean motherhood, making Ecuador a diverse but vulnerable country to climate change (Republic of Ecuador, 2025) According to projections from the

title: JRC143555_02

Most days are expected to have climatic conditions similar to the present, albeit with regional variations. In addition, glacier decline has been significant, with a loss of around 50 % of glaciers ’ surface over the last 50 years (Republic of Ecuador, 2025) Climate change is altering climate patterns in Ecuador, increasing the frequency and intensity of forest fires, especially in regions such as the Sierra and the Amazon. As a result, electricity cuts of up to 14 hours per day occurred in 2024, severely affecting the population and productive sectors. Research activities aimed at improving fire handling The increasing incidence of forest fires in Ecuador poses complex challenges that go beyond the environment, directly affecting the country’s safety, health, livelihoods and natural and cultural heritage. Faced with this reality, the IFM is a strategic tool to tackle this problem in a preventive, coordinated and sustainable way, integrating the ecological, social, cultural and economic dimensions of the fire in the territory. In this context, scientific research becomes a key pillar for understanding fire dynamics across the country’s different ecosystems, as well as for designing innovative, contextualised and evidence-based solutions. text: 93 2.8. Mexico Fire has historically been a key natural element in the dynamics of terrestrial ecosystems. Their presence influences the structure, functioning and dynamics of terrestrial ecosystems (Villers- Ruiz, 2009), especially in areas where fire has coexisted for centuries as part of its ecological scheme. However, in the current context, characterised by extensive and inappropriate use of fire by humans and the effects of climate change, their role can be transformed into a factor of degradation and threat to both ecosystems and human communities. In Mexico, 98 % of forest fires are man -made, resulting from agricultural, recreational or inappropriate practices such as the burning of waste and the use of fire in forest and forest interface areas. These fires are mainly concentrated in states with high vegetation cover and forest interface areas, such as Oaxaca, Chiapas, Durango,

title: JRC143555_02
text: terface areas. These fires are mainly concentrated in states with high vegetation cover and forest interface areas, such as Oaxaca, Chiapas, Durango, Jalisco and the St ate of Mexico, where fuel accumulation conditions and inappropriate use of fire are combined with increasingly extreme climates, leading to massive and severe explosive fires. In this context, Mexico has adopted a more comprehensive vi sion through regulatory and strategic planning instruments. NOM -015- SEMARNAT/AGRICULTURA-2023, for example, establishes the lines for controlled use of fire on forest and agricultural land. Its purpose is to prevent and reduce unwanted forest fires by regulating burning practices, promoting a culture of co-responsibility and safety. This programme recognises fire not only as an agent that impacts on the health of ecosystems, but also as a management tool with ecological, social and economic benefits, provided that it is used with technical knowledge and under safe conditions. This promotes science -based management of fire, community involvement and capacity building at all levels of government. The comprehensive management of fire in Mexico is now a crucial ch allenge in the face of the effects of climate change and the need to conserve our ecosystems. Understanding the ecology of fire and promoting its responsible use will reduce the impacts of harmful fires. 2.8.1. Fire danger in 2024 Fire hazard refers to the likelihood of a forest fire spreading. This criterion considers various factors such as temperature, relative humidity, dryness of fuels, wind speed and direction (Veneto, 2000; Blind, 1998). It

It can also be defined as the set of environmental variables, fuel characteristics and ground conditions that determine the possibility of spreading, persistence and damage to vegetation (Dentoni et al., 2012; CONAFOR, 2010). As part of the process of continuous monitoring and evaluation of these variables, the CONAFOR has developed the Forest Fire Hazard Prediction System (SPPIF) , an online consultation tool targeting institutions of the three government orders, non-governmental organisations and civil society. One of the components of the SPPIF is the fire hazard mapping, which pr ovides for the combination of factors that favour the spread and intensity of the fire, including its extreme behaviour, depending on the quantity and type of biomass available. In tropical and subtropical areas, such as those in most of Mexico, are already observed in longer and more severe fire seasons. As they are not limited by the amount of biomass, but by fuel humidity, and respond rapidly to changes in the climate. Consequently, fires occur more frequently in regions with intermediate humidi ty availability, where dry conditions are frequent enough to intermittently dry the available vegetation, but not sufficiently dry to limit fuel production (Jones et al., 2022). This pattern is very well adapted to Mexico’s ecosystems (low forests, pine and scrub forests), where drought combined with high fuel load generates high fire hazard scenarios. text: 107 2.8.10. Research activities aimed at improving fire handling In Mexico, there is a group of researchers called the Mexican Fire Management Network. It has consolidated itself for the exchange of technical and scientific knowledge between specialists, academic institutions, civil and governmental organisations, made up of experts from across the country, this network promotes applied research and the generation of evidence that supports more effective publ ic policies in the face of forest fires. Within this framework of collaboration, a number of working sessions have been held to establish the priority lines of research on fire management. An important example in this process was the Study Priorities Works hop on Fuego Management in Mexico, carried out in 2008, which defined strategic lines that have guided multiple scientific and technical initiatives on national territory. Environmentally, the fine particles and toxic gases they carry deteriorate air quality, impacting both nearby communities and distant areas. From a health perspective, exposure to these substances, es pecially tiny particles such as PM2.5, is linked to respiratory diseases such

The availability of data has facilitated the development of monitoring and warning systems, which make spatial information available to the public. CONABIO has developed and operated the Forest Fire Early Warning System (SATIF) for Mexico and the Americas Centre ( http://incendios- beta.conabio.gob.mx/), since 1999, providing information mainly to CONAFOR’s management of Fuego Management. Hotspots The main axis of SATIF is active fire monitoring (hotspots), which aims to generate information on early forest fire detection. A hotspot is considered to be any heat source on the earth’s surface, which emits sufficient temperature to be recorded by a sensor,

title: JRC143555_02
text: t fire detection. A hotspot is considered to be any heat source on the earth’s surface, which emits sufficient temperature to be recorded by a sensor, to be detected as a temperature anomaly. The heat source can be caused by fires, agricultural burns, hot soils due to sunshine, active volcanoes and anthropogenic sources (gas flames in oil wells, solar panels, opencast mines, metal structures) etc. Under this concept and the method used for detection, there is no certainty about the number of fires, nor their size, because it is not certain that each hotspot corresponds to a forest fire or other source. CONABIO has the Satellite Image Reception System (SRIS) where it receives Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) data, the data are used for the detection of hotspots. The mapping used at this stage is updated according to its availability. Hotspots that are continuously detected are called stable hotspots, which are mainly associated with anthropogenic activities and volcanic activity. The entire process, from receiving the signal sent by the satellite at CONABIO's SRIS, processing it to obtain the image, applying algorithms to extract hot spots, characterising the site, publishing it on the system's website and sending the information by email to interested users, is carried out automatically in an average time of 30 min

text: 116 2.9. Paraguay 2.9.1. Fire danger in 2024 The danger of forest fires in Paraguay is determined by a combination of environmental factors and human activities. Environmental factors include high temperatures and low rainfall during the dry season, which reduce soil moisture and vegetation, creating conditions conducive to the spread of fire. In Paraguay, forest fires are more frequent in the dry season (June to October), when vegetation humidity is low ( Figure 77) and temperatures vary. In addition, strong winds can fuel flame and spread the fire at high speed. On the other hand, factors related to human activities play a crucial role, as the burning of grasslands for agriculture and livestock farming, often without proper control, is one of the main causes of fires in the country. Activities such as land use change, poaching and lack of proper handling in rural areas, where a minimal

title: JRC143555_02
text: e of the main causes of fires in the country. Activities such as land use change, poaching and lack of proper handling in rural areas, where a minimal source of ignition can lead to large-scale fires, are also influenced.” The combination of these variables makes certain regions particularly vulnerable to fires, highlighting the importance of preventive measures and constant monitoring. In 2024, Paraguay faced one of the most critical forest fire seasons, with thousands of hectares affected in different regions of the country. The combination of extreme temperatures, prolonged drought and strong winds created conditions conducive to the spread of fire, especially in areas with high dry vegetation. This was compounded by human factors such as the uncontrolled burning of grassland for agricultural 11 Heat sources recorded by sensors NOAA-20 VIIRS, NOAA-21 VIIRS and S -NPP VIIRS, 375 m. pur

The Western Region or Chaco Paraguayo and the northern part of the Eastern Region were the areas most affected during the months of August to October, with a severe impact on ecosystems, wildlife and local communities. Against this background, the institution s stepped up monitoring and response efforts. 2.9.2. Causes of fires During 2024, the spread of forest fires in Paraguay was the result of a combination of extreme climatic conditions and anthropic practices associated with the use of fire, mainly in rural areas. The prolonged absence of rainfall, together with temperatures above historical averages, created an environment conducive to the rapid spread of fire, especially in areas with dry vegetation. These alterations in climate patterns, with higher temperatures and longer periods of drought, have increased the risk of fires in various regions of the country. Research also suggests the use of fire as a management tool in agricultural activities, using techniques such as the burning of grasslands, direct burning of stubble or vegetation, and the use of strings or hills for the disposal of woody waste. Fire prevention activities and information campaigns In 2024, forest fire prevention strategies were strengthened through a number of initiatives aimed at reducing risks and raising public awareness. As part of these actions, strict measures were put in place for the control of the use of fire in areas exposed to the occurrence of forest fires, based on climate reports that warned about above-average temperatures and conditions conducive to the spread of fires. The National Forestry Institute (INFONA) of Paraguay issued resolutions on the prohibition of the use of fire in various types of areas such as grassland, scrub, shrubs, forest plantations, crops or other vegetation.

Medical emergencies increased in the most affected areas, where dense smoke reduced air quality to dangerous levels. Many patients experienced dizziness, extreme fatigue and dehydration, increasing the burden on health care centres. In 2024, the picture has not been different, as the number of fires has increased considerably in several regions of the country. The risk of fires is largely determined by bioclimatic factors, such as reduced rainfall and prolonged droughts, particularly in the Andes and the Amazon. According to the Peruvian National Meteorology and Hydrology Service (SENAMHI), for 2024, there was a marked difference in climatic conditions along Peruvian territory: while the northern saw experienced a significant reduction in rainfall, the central and southern saw recorded higher than normal rainfall, which details the following: — The Sierra Norte area, from July to November, has had persistent dry conditions, with episodes of moderate to extreme drought. The persistence of dry conditions in the saw was influenced by atmospheric circulation at high and medium levels of the atmosphere. In particular, the predominance of western wind flows, which reduced the moisture concentration in the region, was identified. text: 140 2.10.5. Fire-fighting facilities Fighting forest fires in Peru is a multisectoral effort, involving various state entities, specialised institutions and the local population itself. The Peruvian Armed Forces, including the Army and Air Force, play a crucial role in fighting forest fires. Helicopters equipped with the bambi Bucket system, a flexible container that accurately transports and discharges water over fire sites, have been deployed. Each bambi Bucket can store up to 3 000 litres of water, allowing multiple flights per day to fight forest fires. As part of the UFMS of the SERFOR Directorate- General for Forest Information and Management and Wildlife Fauna issues daily reports of hotspots and distributes them to local, regional, rural and indigenous communities, as well as to institutions involved in forest fire risk management. Causes of fires In Peru, various causes of forest fires are identified, which can be categorised according to the regions of the country. Amazon Region In the Amazon, there has been notable growth in the commercial agricultural sector, especially in extensive crops such as African palm (Elaeis guineensis), cocoa (Theobroma cacao) and various fruits. This increase has created the need to clear forested land to expand agricultural activity, thereby changing land use. In addition, the construction of new roads, considered key links for the region's economic development, is driving migratory agriculture, one

title: JRC143555_02
text: and use. In addition, the construction of new roads, considered key links for the region's economic development, is driving migratory agriculture, one of the main causes of deforestation. In an effort to start new plantings in deforested areas, burning is carried out which, if not properly controlled, can turn into forest fires. In all activities that use fire to remove native vegetation residues, there is a risk that it will get out of control, affecting forested areas and other wild vegetation ecosystems. Andean Region In Andean ecosystems, where the vegetation composition favours the spread of fire, forest fires can reach catastrophic proportions. In this region, grasslands are one of the few sources of food for livestock, which leads to periodic burning to renew them, as they are more palatable to cattle. However, when these practices are not controlled, they can lead to fires that c

However, when these practices are not controlled, they can lead to fires that cause the loss of plant associations, including natural pastures. Forest fires affect both the population and ecosystem services, in many cases reaching disaster levels and harming both human communities and the benefits provided by the forest. Exotic species such as eucalyptus (Eucalyptus globulus) and pine (Pinus radiata) are widely used in plantations up to 3 800 metres above sea level. These species are pyrophilic due to the presence of volatile oils in eucalyptus leaves and resins in pine trees, which facilitates the accumulation of litter that is difficult to decompose and, therefore, the spread of forest fires. This situation is exacerbated during periods

In addition, in the high Andean wetlands, there is a high incidence of fires caused by the burn ing of totora (emergent aquatic flora), as in the case of Lake Titicaca, which causes the loss of flora and habitats for wildlife.. Interandina Region In the transition zone between the Andean region and the Amazon (forest edge), cloud forests and other types of plant associations are threatened by the use of fire in land management. This activity is one of the most significant in this type of terrain, which has extreme topography and is home to a significant population. North Region In this region of the country, fires are mainly caused by people known as ‘mieleros’, who collect honey from wild bees. Injury and loss of life The forest fires in Peru in 2024 have had a significant impact on the population and the environment, leaving an alarming balance of casualties and damage. According to the National Institute of Civil Defence (INDECI), fires killed 35 people in different r egions of the country, becoming one of the most lethal years in terms of forest disasters in recent history. In addition to the loss of life, 285 people were reported injured, many of them with severe burns and respiratory conditions due to exposure to smoke. Thousands of people were directly and indirectly affected, with forced evacuations an

text: evere burns and respiratory conditions due to exposure to smoke. Thousands of people were directly and indirectly affected, with forced evacuations and significant material losses. In response to this emergency, the Peruvian government declared a state of emergency in 46 districts of 23 provinces, located in six departments: Amazonas, Cajel, Huánuco, Lambayeque, Saint Martin and Ucayali. This measure allowed for the mobilisation of resources for fire control and for the attention of the affected population. The National Forestry and Wildlife Servi ce (SERFOR), as the National Forestry and Wildlife Authority, carried out a preliminary inventory of wildlife affected by forest fires. It is estimated that 709 vertebrate species were impacted in various ecozones in the country, distributed as follows: Low forest (377 specie s), high selva (204 species) and Sierra (128 species). In terms of birds, individuals were reported from species such as nictibium (Nyctib ius griseus), Azara pijui (Synallaxis azarae) and ear -white solitary (Entomodestes leucotis). Mutual assistance operations In 2024, the Peruvian Government, through the Ministry of Defence and in coordination with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, deployed aircraft and specialised staff to support the monitoring and extinction of a large -scale forest fire in the province of Loja, Ecuador. text: 144 2.10.10. Climate change In Peru, between 2017 and 2024, the area affected by forest fires has shown an increasing trend, with particularly notable increases in 2020, 2022 and 2024. In the last year, the highest figure was recorded, with 777 373.05 ha burnt, a significant increase compared to previous years. In parallel, the number of fires has followed a similar evolution, with a considerable increase since 2020. In 2024, approximately 24 800 incidents were recorded, in stark contrast to the 5 541 fires reported in 2017. This data shows a worrying trend, possibly linked to the effects of climate change. Factors such as rising temperatures, prolonged droughts and reduced rainfall are contributing to both the frequency and intensity of forest fires, even in areas previously c onsidered to be of low vulnerability. The occurrence of fires in high biodiversity areas, such as the Peruvian

title: JRC143555_02

The occurrence of fires in high biodiversity areas, such as the Peruvian Amazon, poses a significant risk to ecosystem integrity and species conservation. Faced with this scenario, the 2025 -2027 Multisectoral Forest Fi re Plan is a key tool, aligned with national policies such as the National Disaster Risk Management Policy 2050 and PLANAGERD 2022 – 2030, and constitutes a specific response by the State to the new risk scenarios generated or intensified by climate change. In this regard, its implementation allows: — Mitigating the effects of climate change: Preventive and planned interventions aim to reduce the emission of greenhouse gases and particles from biomass burning, thereby reducing the carbon footprint in the affected ecosystems. — Strengthening resilience and adaptive capacity: Multi -sectoral articu

title: JRC143555_02
text: ss burning, thereby reducing the carbon footprint in the affected ecosystems. — Strengthening resilience and adaptive capacity: Multi -sectoral articulation drives risk mitigation measures that allow communities to adapt to new climate scenarios, minimising the impact of extreme events such as forest fires. In short, t he Plan promotes actions aimed at improving knowledge and monitoring of risk, strengthening preventive capacities and increasing the level of emergency preparedness, which contributes significantly to mitigating the impacts of climate change. It also foste rs adaptive management that protects both ecosystems and people’s livelihoods, consolidating a comprehensive approach to sustainable and resilient development. 2.10.11. However, these have a high occurrence at the same time. In other words, although fires do not spread over large areas and do not exceed 48 to 72 hours on average until they are controlled, they are simultaneously cleared by limiting response capacities. The pea k season for forest and field fires in Uruguay is determined by climatic conditions related to high temperatures and droughts. It is regulated by Decree No. 436/007, which establishes in Article 2 that ‘From 1 November of each year until 30 April of the fo llowing year, it is prohibited to light fires or burn anything outdoors anywhere in the national territory.’ https://www.impo.com.uy/bases/decretos/436- 2007. Fire-fighting facilities The National Fire Service has a total of 71 operational detachments throughout the country. These detachments have light first -response units for forest fires, as well as vehicles for urban fires, equipped with the necessary materials and equipment to respond to a forest fire. In terms of human resources, the DNB has more than 1 300 officials distributed among the va rious operational units. As part of the Annual Training Plan, they are trained in forest firefighting, and the Firefighters' Specialised School also provides annual training and education in this area with different levels of courses. These firefighters are specially trained and equipped to fight forest fires. As part of the summer fire plan, SOPRIF is established annually. One of its objectives is to establish coordination mechanisms between all state agencies and organised civil society to fulfil the strategic objectives set, seeking to optimise response capacity during the summer season by increasing and redistributing resources to improve the quality of the response. text: 154 3. Global Fire Information System (GWIS) This section describes the evolution of fires in 2024 by comparing with the fire campaigns in previous years. Fire information has been generated from the product of Near-Real-Time (NRT) burnt areas in GWIS, which is based on the combined use of thermal anomalies ( hotspots) of the MODIS and VIIRS sensors to delineate the perimeters of each fire, and which is then used to determine the areas burned by the fires. The seasonality of fires and their trends are found in the Country Profile and Current Statistics Portal applications available on GWIS. The following sections present information on fire analysis based on NRT data in GWIS and have the same format for each country. It is important to stress that these data include fires in all types of green cover, not just forests, and that they have an intrinsic limitation linked to the spatial resol

title: JRC143555_02
text: ss that these data include fires in all types of green cover, not just forests, and that they have an intrinsic limitation linked to the spatial resolution of the space sensors used. These data may not correspond exactly to the data reported by the national systems of the countries in the previous sections of this report. However, the robust method used to determine the number of fires and burnt area allows these data to be used to determine fire trends and their impact on countries in the Latin American and Caribbean region (LAC). The format of the chapters in each country is as follows: 1. Map of burnt areas detected during 2024, and summary. 2. Weekly trend graphs, presented first for each week and then with cumulative data (grey area shows maximum and minimum average over recent years). The blue line is the average of previous years. title: JRC143555_02
text: 203 4. Conclusions 2024 was characterized by a significant increase in the frequency and severity of forest fires in the LAC region. Human action, due to the improper use of fire and other activities such as agricultural expansion, is considered the main factor, although countries have reported that extreme climatic conditions, influenced by the topography and bioclimatic characteristics of the region, contributed to the emergence and spread of these events. This highlights the vulnerability of the various bioclimatic areas to natural disasters, which is a growing concern among countries. In the context of firefighting, countries have made significant progress such as developing technologies and tools for early detection, which is key to enable a more effective and efficient response to forest fires. In this regard, the IFM has been highlighted as a strategic tool to tackle the problem i

title: JRC143555_02
text: able a more effective and efficient response to forest fires. In this regard, the IFM has been highlighted as a strategic tool to tackle the problem in a preventive, coordinated and sustainable manner. Countries have presented different programmes and actions that strengthen the focus of the IFM, raising awareness of its benefits and positive results. A number of legislative and regulatory initiatives aimed at promoting effective management of the climate crisis and fostering inter-institutional articulation have also been implemented. These initiatives include specific measures for fire management, reflecting the commitment of countries in the region to comprehensively address the challenges caused by forest fires. The intentional fire scenario presents a significant challenge due to the increase of simultaneous events in critical areas and moments, hampering control actions and can exh

title: JRC143555_02
text: nario presents a significant challenge due to the increase of simultaneous events in critical areas and moments, hampering control actions and can exhaust available resources. The report stresses the importance of strengthening research into causes, as well as carrying out fire risk assessments, taking into account geographical and climate diversity. Investing in effective planning and implementation of activities, by strengthening existing means and equipment and inter-institutional articulation, becomes a strategic priority for the countries of the region. The promotion of applied research on fire management is also seen as an essential element in understanding the complexities of fire in the various ecosystems, optimising decision-making or designing more effective public policies. Countries agree that it is essential to carry out environmental education and awareness programmes, invo
